newsitem.title: USA: Calif prison officials seen pressing for new bonds.
newsitem.headline: Calif prison officials seen pressing for new bonds.

text.p: California prison officials are expected to press state lawmakers in early 1997 to authorize the sale of billions of dollars of lease revenue bonds to house the state's growing prison population, state officials said on Thursday.
"We need to get something done. We need to get something quickly," J.P. Tremblay, assistant secretary of the state Youth and Adult Correctional Agency, said in an interview.

Tremblay said his agency would likely seek the authority to sell up to $2 billion in lease revenue bonds because they can be issued more quickly than general obligation bonds, which would require voter approval.

"Our opening offer will likely be 'We need lease revenue bonds' because we need the money now," Tremblay said. "But we may go for a combination of lease revenue and general obligation bonds, whatever we can get through the Legislature."

Governor Pete Wilson's administration had proposed placing on the November ballot nearly $3 billion in general obligation bonds to finance construction of state prisons and other local and state criminal justice facilities.
Of that money, $1.87 billion would have gone to the Department of Corrections to build six new prisons.
But state legislators only agreed to place about $700 million of general obligation bonds on the November ballot to build local jail and other facilities.
"We are looking at 1998 and 1999 when we will physically run out of room to put everybody," Tremblay said.
"We're running out of room. We're running out of time," he added.

The state currently houses over 142,000 prisoners in adult facilities and another 10,100 wards in juvenile facilities. The population is projected to grow quickly as a result of "three strikes" legislation, which increases sentences for repeat offenders.
To issue lease revenue bonds, the Department of Corrections would need only legislative approval and the governor's signature, Tremblay said.
Issuing general obligation bonds would be more time consuming since the department would have to get both legislative and voter approval to sell the debt, he added.
Wilson spokesman Sean Walsh said the Republican governor was likely to ask the Legislature again next year to place general obligation bonds for prisons on the state ballot.
"We'll be back to the Legislature next year trying to get additional prisons," Walsh said.
